meta.title: Twelve questions, twelve base pairs
meta.intro: Every correct answer completes a pair in the helix. Every wrong one leaves a mismatch you can trace back to its chapter.

ratings.message: Every rung matched. You read the study closely.

ratings.message: A couple of mismatches. The chapters below will close the gaps.

ratings.message: You have the core ideas. Revisit the chapters below to fix the rest.

questions.question: How many hydrogen bonds hold a G–C base pair together?

options.text: Two
Three
Four
One

questions.explanation: G always pairs with C, joined by three hydrogen bonds. A pairs with T through two. That fixed rule is how a cell copies the ladder without losing the message.

questions.question: Why are human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) the most contested stem cell source?

options.text: They can only become one cell type
Collecting them destroys early-stage embryos
They are taken from adult skin
They always cause tumours after transplant

questions.explanation: hESCs come from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst, so harvesting them destroys the embryo. Moral views on that differ between countries, which has delayed hESC-based therapies.

questions.question: What separates somatic from germ-line gene therapy?

options.text: Somatic changes affect only the person treated; germ-line changes can pass to descendants
Somatic therapy uses viruses and germ-line therapy never does
Somatic changes are permanent, germ-line changes fade over time
Somatic therapy edits embryos, germ-line therapy edits blood cells

questions.explanation: A change in body cells affects one patient. A germ-line change would be inherited, which is why the study treats it as an ethical red line.

questions.question: In December 2023 the FDA approved Casgevy, the first CRISPR/Cas9 therapy. What does it treat?

options.text: Parkinson's disease
Hereditary angioedema
Severe sickle cell disease
Macular degeneration

questions.explanation: Casgevy edits the BCL11A enhancer in a patient's blood stem cells to reactivate fetal hemoglobin. Lyfgenia, a lentiviral therapy approved the same month, treats the same disease.

questions.question: How do induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) avoid the embryo problem?

options.text: They are made by reprogramming adult cells, such as skin cells, into an embryonic-like state
They are collected from the placenta after birth
They are grown from animal embryos instead
They come from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst

questions.explanation: Defined transcription factors push adult cells back to pluripotency, so no embryo is destroyed. The trade-off is risk: undifferentiated iPSCs can form teratomas after transplantation.

questions.question: In the Kyoto Parkinson's trial, what happened to dopamine synthesis at 24 months?

options.text: It rose 63.5% in the high-dose group against 7.0% in the low-dose group
It rose 7.0% in the high-dose group against 63.5% in the low-dose group
It rose about 50% in both groups
It did not change in either group

questions.explanation: Seven patients received iPSC-derived dopaminergic progenitors, and 4 of 6 evaluable patients improved significantly. The gap between the two doses is a clear dose response, which turns dose into an equity question.

questions.question: What makes a base editor different from standard CRISPR-Cas9 cutting?

options.text: It cuts both DNA strands twice for extra accuracy
It carries a whole new gene inside a viral shell
It converts one DNA letter into another without a double-strand break
It only works on embryos

questions.explanation: A base editor fuses a modified Cas9 to a deaminase, so it rewrites a single letter without cutting through both strands. That avoids the most dangerous repair outcomes, but it cannot fix insertions, deletions or triplet repeats.

questions.question: What did He Jiankui announce at the Second International Summit on Human Genome Editing in 2018?

options.text: The first approved CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease
That he had edited human embryos, producing twins with intended HIV resistance
A global ban on all gene editing
A method for making iPSCs from skin cells

questions.explanation: His claims were unverified, and the organizers condemned the work as irresponsible. The summit did not call for a blanket ban. It pointed toward a rigorous, responsible pathway for any future trials.

questions.question: Why is consent the decisive argument against germ-line editing, even with safer tools?

options.text: Future generations inherit the edit and cannot be asked to agree
Editing tools are too inaccurate to ever be used
Embryos cannot survive being edited
Regulators have not yet reviewed any germ-line research

questions.explanation: A safer editor does not resolve the objection. The people who would carry the edit are not yet born, and no current governance mechanism can obtain their consent.

questions.question: Sickle cell disease causes roughly 300,000 to 400,000 births a year. Where do over 80% of them occur?

options.text: North America
Sub-Saharan Africa
Western Europe
East Asia

questions.explanation: Meanwhile U.S. list prices sit near $2.2 million for Casgevy and $3.1 million for Lyfgenia per patient. A cure that exists is not yet a cure that arrives where the need is greatest.

questions.chapterLabel: From one body to an ecosystem
questions.question: Why does the forest chapter say heritable edits matter beyond a single patient?

options.text: A change made to one organism can travel through the species around it
Forests are the main source of therapeutic stem cells
Edited genes cannot survive outside a laboratory
Ecosystems are already covered by strict gene-editing law

questions.explanation: No genome lives alone. Each one sits inside a web of other lives, so heritable edits raise the same question at the scale of a whole ecosystem.

questions.question: Which instrument ties Medicaid payment for sickle cell gene therapies to outcomes, with rebates if treatment does not fully work?

options.text: The WHO genome editing framework
The Oviedo Convention
India's centralised licensing authority
The CMS Cell and Gene Therapy Access Model

questions.explanation: Outcome-based payment turns the question "does this work?" into a contractual condition. The WHO framework is non-binding advice, and the Oviedo Convention prohibits heritable genome modification.
